name: What This Means for Each Reader
title: What This Means for Each Reader
answer: This idea says that schools should begin AI adoption with adult work and clear governance, not with student assignments. Teachers try approved tools on their own tasks first, leaders decide which tools and data are allowed, and families ask how AI is used and whether the child can explain the learning. It matters because it keeps human judgment, data control, and student thinking at the center while schools learn what the tools can and cannot do.

crumbs.name: What AI Can and Cannot Do

sections.body: The idea is a staged approach to AI in schools. It starts with teachers using an approved tool to draft routine materials such as a parent email, practice questions, or a lower level reading passage, then checking and editing the result. That lets staff see where the tool helps and where it stumbles before students use it. When students do use AI, the assignment should be designed so that the mental work remains the student's. The problem it solves is rushing AI into classrooms without knowing its limits, without approved tools, or without clear ownership of decisions.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the classroom, the text directs teachers to begin with their own workload rather than student assignments. They use an approved school tool to draft a parent email, practice questions, or a reading passage at a lower level, then check and edit what it gives them. The text does not give grade bands for this practice. Principals and district leaders decide which tools are approved, what data may go into them, and who owns each decision in Figure 1.6. They train staff before rollout and measure results before scaling, while school board members ask oversight questions and parents ask which tools their child uses and what happens to the information typed into them.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text does not attach a research evidence label to this idea. It offers a policy snapshot and examples instead. It states that as of June 2026, somewhere between 35 and 37 states plus Puerto Rico had issued AI guidance for schools, depending on who is counting, and that Ohio went further by requiring every district to adopt an AI policy by July 1, 2026 (Playlab, 2026; Ohio Department of Education and Workforce, 2026). It also points to Figure 1.6 for decision ownership and to the Los Angeles story as a reason for boards to ask about vendors and data. No study, effect size, or classroom trial is given in the supplied text, so this idea rests on policy and practice rather than research evidence.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets limits on what AI should do. Teachers must check and edit any draft, and assignments must be built so that students still perform the thinking. Leaders keep decisions about approved tools, allowed data, and who owns each decision in Figure 1.6, and they should train staff before rollout and measure results before scaling. Board members hold oversight, not tool selection, and they should ask what problem AI addresses, how the district will judge success, which student data enters the tool and where that data is sent, and which choices remain with a human. Parents should ask which tools their child uses and what happens to the information typed in, and they can ask the child to explain the work in their own words; if the child cannot explain it, the tool may have done the learning instead. The text adds that many tools named in the Volume carry age limits and parental consent rules, and later chapters list these for each product.
